deduction_findings.explanation: Your room cost ₹8,000/day against a limit of ₹5,000/day, so the policy lets the insurer pay 62.5% of room rent, nursing charges, medical practitioners' fees and operation theatre charges. That comes to a deduction of ₹19,500. The insurer cut ₹42,300, which means it also applied the cut to medicines and tests, which this clause doesn't allow. You can challenge ₹22,800.

similar_cases.forum: State Commission Gujarat (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Gujarat State, Ahmedabad)
similar_cases.insurer_reason: Room rent eligibility was 1% of sum insured (Rs 3,000/day) and a higher room was taken, so proportionate deduction applied; the silver plan carries a 10% co-payment; nursing and non-medical items not payable; OT consumables and procedure charges included in OT charges.
similar_cases.reasoning: The State Commission found that the policy wording justified only four deductions: excess room rent (Rs 3,000), nursing charges (Rs 1,050), non-medical items (Rs 6,456) and the 10% co-payment on implants (Rs 16,065), totalling Rs 26,571. The insurer could not justify the proportionate cuts on surgeon/doctor fees, investigations, gases and physiotherapy or the 'included in OT' deductions (Rs 65,792), which amounted to deficiency in service. The District Commission's award was reduced from Rs 92,363 to Rs 65,792.

similar_cases.forum: State Commission Karnataka (Karnataka State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Bengaluru)
similar_cases.insurer_reason: Claim settled as per Mediclaim 2012 terms: room rent restricted to 1% of sum insured per day with proportionate deduction of other charges, consumables non-payable, and only 80% of the admissible claim payable for an insured over 55 years without 48 months of claim-free continuous cover.
similar_cases.reasoning: Relying on the Supreme Court's decision in Jacob Punnen v. United India Insurance (2021), the Commission held that the insurer had not notified this long-standing policyholder of the revised, more restrictive terms before renewal, so settling the claim on those terms was deficient. It also relied on the NCDRC ruling in New India Assurance v. A.K. Kariappa that applying a mechanical proportionate deduction, instead of finding out what the hospital would have charged for the eligible room category, is a faulty procedure. The insurer was directed to pay up to the Rs 3,00,000 sum insured less the amount paid (Rs 1,76,029) with 6% interest, Rs 25,000 compensation and Rs 10,000 costs.

similar_cases.insurer_reason: ICU charges of Rs 8,750/day exceeded the ICU limit of 2% of sum insured per day, so all other hospital expenses except medicines were paid in the same proportion under clause 3.2 (proportionate deduction); remaining deductions were non-medical items under Annexure 2.
similar_cases.reasoning: The Forum accepted the hospital tariff showing that all charges other than the bed charge were the same whether the patient was in a ward or the ICU. Disallowing room rent above the limit and non-medical items was in order, but reducing other charges proportionately when the hospital has no class-based tariff was held unjustified and against IRDAI guidelines; the insurer itself conceded that proportionate deduction would not apply to doctor fees and investigations at this hospital. The balance admissible expenses deducted proportionately were ordered to be paid (amount not quantified in the award).

similar_cases.insurer_reason: Excess room and nursing charges disallowed (eligible Rs 3,000/day); doctor fees and hospital service charges paid in proportion to the eligible room rent under policy condition 3.1; diet charges not payable; PPE kits paid for only one day for a non-Covid patient; investigation charges lacked a break-up. On reassessment the TPA found a further Rs 6,538 payable.
similar_cases.reasoning: The Forum held that deducting diet charges, excess room charges and the proportionate reduction of other charges were as per policy terms and in order. However, disallowing PPE kit charges during Covid times was not justified even for a non-Covid patient, and the additional investigation bills had to be considered. The insurer was directed to pay the PPE deduction, the admissible investigation charges and the Rs 6,538 it had already found payable.

similar_cases.forum: State Commission West Bengal (West Bengal State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kolkata)
similar_cases.insurer_reason: Clause 3.1(d): room rent, boarding and nursing limited to 1% of sum insured per day (2% for ICU/ICCU); if the room rate exceeds the limit, all other hospital expenses except medicines are paid in the same proportion as the admissible rate bears to the actual room rate.
similar_cases.reasoning: Reading clause 3.1(d), the Commission held that once a patient is admitted to a room/ICU above the entitled category, all admissible expenses other than medicines are reimbursable at proportionate rates and not at actuals. It found no inaccuracy in the TPA's deductions and held that the complainant had misread the policy, so no relief was granted.

similar_cases.forum: State Commission West Bengal (West Bengal State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kolkata)
similar_cases.insurer_reason: The patient occupied rooms above her entitlement, so room rent was capped and doctor, nursing and other expenses were reimbursed proportionately; doctor fees paid directly outside the hospital bill were not reimbursed.
similar_cases.reasoning: The Commission upheld the room-rent deduction of Rs 12,950 as fully justified by the 1%-of-sum-insured cap (Rs 4,250 x 5 days). But it found the proportionate deductions were wrongly computed - for example, on a day when the room was 21.29% above eligibility, 52.77% of the OT equipment charge was deducted - and held that doctor fees paid directly could not be refused without written reasons, given the insurer's own head-office guideline. The insurer was ordered to recompute, pay the balance with 9% interest, furnish a calculation sheet and pay Rs 25,000 litigation costs.

escalation.title: Write to the insurer's grievance officer
escalation.action: Send the complaint letter ClaimBack drafts, listing each disputed amount and the clause or rule behind it. Keep proof of sending.
escalation.deadline_note: The insurer must acknowledge immediately and resolve it within 14 days, by 01 Oct 2026.

escalation.title: Register it on Bima Bharosa
escalation.action: Also log the complaint on IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal (bimabharosa.irdai.gov.in) so it's tracked.
escalation.deadline_note: Optional, but it puts the complaint on IRDAI's record.

escalation.title: Go to the Insurance Ombudsman, Bengaluru
escalation.action: If the insurer rejects your complaint, doesn't reply, or replies unsatisfactorily, file with the Ombudsman online at cioins.co.in. It's free.
escalation.deadline_note: Possible after 30 days without a satisfactory reply. File within 1 year of the insurer's reply. Claims up to Rs 50 lakh.

escalation.title: Consumer commission (last resort)
escalation.action: If the Ombudsman route doesn't work for you, a district consumer commission can hear the dispute. You can't pursue both for the same dispute.
escalation.deadline_note: General information only; consider advice before filing.

NIVA-AS-4.1-PRORATA.title: Proportionate deduction limited to associated medical expenses
NIVA-AS-4.1-PRORATA.quote: If the Insured Person is admitted in a room / ICU / ICCU at rates exceeding the aforesaid limits, then We shall be liable to pay only a pro-rated portion of the total Associated Medical Expenses (including surcharge or taxes thereon) as per the following formula: (eligible Room limit / Room Rent actually incurred) * total Associated Medical Expenses Associated Medical Expenses shall include Room Rent, nursing charges, Medical Practitioners' fees and operation theatre charges
NIVA-AS-4.1-PRORATA.source: Arogya Sanjeevani Policy, Niva Bupa Health Insurance Co. Ltd.

Intensive Care Unit (ICU) / Intensive Cardiac Care Unit (ICCU) expenses up to 5% of sum insured subject to maximum of Rs. 10,000/- per day.

grievance.subject: Grievance: claim no. CLM-NHI-26-0791240, policy no. NHI/AS/2025/0419087
grievance.body:
Date: 17 September 2026

To
The Grievance Redressal Officer
Nirmaan Health Insurance Co. Ltd.

Subject: Grievance against deductions in claim no. CLM-NHI-26-0791240, policy no. NHI/AS/2025/0419087

Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing about the above claim for the hospitalisation of Rajesh Kumar at Greenfield Hospital from 14 July 2026 to 19 July 2026 (Community-acquired pneumonia, right lower lobe). Your office settled the claim by letter dated 04 August 2026, paying ₹66,975 against ₹1,16,100 claimed.

I have checked the decision against the policy wording (Arogya Sanjeevani Policy, Niva Bupa Health Insurance Co. Ltd. (UIN NBHHLIP27056V042627)) and IRDAI's regulations, and I dispute the following:

1. Room rent and associated hospital charges: ₹22,800 of the ₹42,300 deducted as "Proportionate deduction - room rent Rs 8,000/day exceeds eligible Rs 5,000/day (62.5% payable)". The room cost ₹8,000/day against a limit of ₹5,000/day, so the policy lets the insurer pay 62.5% of room rent, nursing charges, medical practitioners' fees and operation theatre charges. That comes to a deduction of ₹19,500. The insurer cut ₹42,300, which means it also applied the cut to medicines and tests, which this clause doesn't allow. I dispute ₹22,800. (Ref: Policy wording: Section 4.1(i)-(ii), Section 4.1, Note 2; IRDAI Master Circular on Protection of Policyholders' Interests, 2024: Schedule C, para 3.1(ix), Section 2, Chapter IV, para 16.3)

I request you to pay the wrongly deducted ₹22,800 (about ₹21,660 after co-payment), and to reply with reasons that refer to the specific terms of the policy. I understand IRDAI requires grievances to be acknowledged immediately and resolved within 14 days. If the grievance is not resolved, I will approach the Insurance Ombudsman under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017.

Enclosures: policy schedule, hospital bill, discharge summary, your settlement letter dated 04 August 2026.

Yours faithfully,
Rajesh Kumar
Policy no. NHI/AS/2025/0419087

(Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017 (as amended up to 09.11.2023; CIO consolidated copy), Rule 14(3)(a) (as amended by G.S.R. 147(E) dated 02.03.2021))

5. Grounds of complaint:

1. Room rent and associated hospital charges: ₹22,800 of the ₹42,300 deducted as "Proportionate deduction - room rent Rs 8,000/day exceeds eligible Rs 5,000/day (62.5% payable)". The room cost ₹8,000/day against a limit of ₹5,000/day, so the policy lets the insurer pay 62.5% of room rent, nursing charges, medical practitioners' fees and operation theatre charges. That comes to a deduction of ₹19,500. The insurer cut ₹42,300, which means it also applied the cut to medicines and tests, which this clause doesn't allow. I dispute ₹22,800. (Ref: Policy wording: Section 4.1(i)-(ii), Section 4.1, Note 2; IRDAI Master Circular on Protection of Policyholders' Interests, 2024: Schedule C, para 3.1(ix), Section 2, Chapter IV, para 16.3)

Relief sought: direct the insurer to pay ₹21,660 (the wrongly deducted amount after co-payment) with interest at bank rate + 2% from the date the claim was reported.

I confirm that the same dispute is not pending before, and has not been decided by, any court, consumer forum or arbitrator.

Enclosures: policy schedule and wording, hospital bill, discharge summary, insurer's letter dated 04 August 2026, my grievance and the insurer's reply (if any).

Yours faithfully,
Rajesh Kumar
